title: Africa: A refining boom on borrowed time
gist: Oxford Economics says the Strait of Hormuz closure has spiked African fuel prices and strengthened the case for domestic refining; capacity could reach ~5.5 mbpd by 2030 in an optimistic case, but Dangote's expansion faces legal disputes and cheap-import competition.

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused sharp increases in fuel prices across Africa, underscoring the need for more domestic refining capacity.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: African import dependence is a macro vulnerability amplified by Gulf disruption.

insights.claim: Many African countries struggle to meet the International Energy Agency's emergency oil stock benchmarks, and the continent remains reliant on imported refined products.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: Supply-security weakness raises fiscal and FX risk when oil spikes.

insights.claim: In an optimistic scenario Africa's refining capacity could reach about 5.5 million barrels per day by 2030, on par with projected demand for refined products.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: Optimistic case implies large import substitution if projects deliver.

insights.claim: Aliko Dangote plans to expand his Lagos refinery to 1.4 mbpd and build a new facility in Lamu, Kenya, but legal disputes and competition from cheaper imports could hinder progress.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: Dangote execution is the swing factor for African refining; the boom is on borrowed time if cheap imports return.
